title: The universe in four big ideas
blurb: Where everything came from, what it’s made of, and what’s out there.

cards.text: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state, and has been expanding ever since. This is the Big Bang theory.
In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the faster they go.
In 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found faint microwaves coming from every direction: leftover heat from the early universe. It won them a Nobel prize.
That afterglow, the cosmic microwave background, is now only about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.

cards.q: About how old is the universe?
cards.explain: About 13.8 billion years. The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.

points: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago
It has been expanding ever since
Its leftover heat still fills the sky

cards.text: The Big Bang made almost nothing but hydrogen and helium. Nearly every other element was made later.
Stars shine by fusing light elements into heavier ones in their cores. The Sun turns hydrogen into helium, releasing huge amounts of energy.
Bigger stars go further, building carbon, oxygen and eventually iron. Fusing iron takes energy instead of releasing it, so it stops there.
When a massive star explodes as a supernova, it scatters these elements into space, where they end up in new stars, planets and people.
Many elements heavier than iron, such as gold, are made in the most violent events of all, including collisions of neutron stars.

cards.q: Where were most elements heavier than helium made?
cards.explain: Inside stars, and in their explosions and collisions.

points: The Big Bang made hydrogen and helium
Stars fuse them into heavier elements
Explosions spread those elements into new worlds

cards.text: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Its edge is called the event horizon.
Black holes come out of Einstein’s general theory of relativity (1915), which describes gravity as mass bending space and time.
Many form when a very massive star runs out of fuel and its core collapses under its own weight.
In April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio telescopes around the world, released the first image of a black hole, in the galaxy M87.
The Milky Way has a black hole at its centre, Sagittarius A*, about four million times the mass of the Sun. It was pictured in 2022.

cards.q: What can’t escape a black hole?
cards.explain: Not even light, which is why they look black.

points: Nothing escapes past the event horizon
They come from Einstein’s theory of gravity
The first images came in 2019 and 2022

cards.text: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. The first ones were confirmed in the early 1990s.
Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b, the first planet around a Sun-like star, in 1995. They shared the 2019 Nobel prize in physics.
Many are found by watching a star dim very slightly as a planet passes in front of it. NASA’s Kepler telescope found thousands this way.
Astronomers have now confirmed more than 5,000 exoplanets.
The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on 25 December 2021, can study the atmospheres of some of these planets.

opts: Seeing their star dim as they pass in front
cards.explain: By the dip in starlight as they cross in front of their star.

points: The first planet around a Sun-like star was found in 1995
Most are spotted by the dimming of their star
Webb can study some of their atmospheres
